Galeazzo served as one of Fontana's official degree promoters for his arts degree (1418) and medical degree (1421). This establishes a direct personal relationship between someone who had spent a decade at Vienna (1394-1405) and the only known Padua physician to create an invented cipher alphabet. Source: Treccani DBI entry for Fontana; Sparavigna (arXiv 1304.4588).

Taught medicine at University of Vienna; personal physician to Duke Albrecht IV of Austria (d.1404). Performed first public anatomical dissection north of the Alps in Vienna in 1404. Source: University of Vienna 650plus, Wikipedia.

Modern scholars identified word-for-word incorporation of Puff's material into Brunschwig's 1500 Small Book without attribution. Puff is NOT cited by name in either the 1500 or 1512 Brunschwig books. The transmission chain is real but invisible at the citation level.

Rudolf likely gave the Voynich to Horcicky, possibly as partial payment for debts. Horcicky's erased signature 'Jacobi a Tepenecz' on fol. 1r (confirmed under UV) dates the transfer to after October 1608 (when Horcicky was ennobled with the 'de Tepenec' title).

Guzy (2022): 500 Taler (= 600 Rheinische Gulden) for 'etlich rare bucher'; only transaction out of 7,000 journal entries matching 600 gold coins. Geizkofler archives, Ludwigsburg. Matches the 600-ducat amount reported by Mnishovsky via Marci.

Horcicky died September 25, 1622. By 1637 Baresch had the manuscript for 'many years.' Both connected to the Clementinum. Missing Jesuit library mark on the Voynich suggests it did not pass through the Jesuit library. The path from Horcicky to Baresch is unconfirmed but the Clementinum connection is suggestive.
Baresch bequeathed his alchemical library, including the Voynich, to his friend Marci. Marci's 1665 letter: 'This book, bequeathed to me by an intimate friend.'
Marci's letter of August 19, 1665 (or 1666) accompanying the manuscript to the Collegio Romano. Via Jesuit mail system.

At least two letters (c. late 1637 via Theodor Moretus S.J.; April 27, 1639). First letter lost; second is earliest surviving mention of the Voynich manuscript (discovered by Zandbergen). Baresch described it as medical, herbal, and chemical.
Rudolf appointed Horcicky as Imperial Chemist (1607), curator of botanical gardens, and personal physician. Ennobled him (1608). Horcicky lent Rudolf enormous sums and received the Melnik estate.
Widemann worked as secretary to Edward Kelley at Rudolf II's court. This places the probable seller of the Voynich within the Prague alchemical circle.
Widemann lived in Rauwolf's former house in Augsburg after Rauwolf's widow died (1597). He was Rauwolf's successor as city physician. Likely handled sale of Rauwolf's remaining books.

Both men were connected to the Clementinum: Horcicky studied and later died there (1598-1622); Baresch earned his BA (1602) and MA (1603) there. This institutional overlap provides a plausible transfer path for the manuscript.

Mnishovsky told Marci that Rudolf paid 600 ducats for the Voynich and that the author was believed to be Roger Bacon. Mnishovsky died in 1644; the information was at minimum 55 years old when Marci relayed it in 1665.

Blotius facilitated transfers of alchemical and magical texts from the Viennese Hofbibliothek to Rudolf's personal collections in Prague. Documents an active institutional channel for manuscript transfer from Vienna to Prague.

Widemann studied at the University of Padua and obtained a doctorate. This places the probable seller of the Voynich at the central institution of our historical network, though a century after the manuscript's creation.

Schaffner trained Horcicky in 'practical techniques such as distillation and the preparation of herbal remedies' at the Jesuit college pharmacy. Schaffner was born in Olomouc — the same city where Brunschwig's Czech translation was published in 1559.
Rauwolf studied medicine under Rondelet at Montpellier. Rondelet reportedly 'introduced alcohol in medicine as an antiseptic and diffused the technique of distillation.'
Clusius studied under Rondelet at Montpellier before Rauwolf. Both were part of a remarkable generation of Rondelet students who became leading European botanists.

Long-term scholarly correspondence. Clusius visited Rauwolf in Augsburg (1565) to examine his herbaria and annotated/corrected plant names. In a letter dated September 7, 1584, Rauwolf asked Clusius to help find a buyer for his plant collections.

Aicholz reported to Camerarius on May 10, 1581 that he had received plant-care instructions from Rauwolf. Documents a connection between Rauwolf and the Vienna medical faculty — the same institution where Puff had been dean a century earlier.
Clusius lived with Aicholz during his time as prefect of the imperial botanical garden in Vienna under Maximilian II.
Rauwolf visited Fuchs at Tubingen on his return from Italy. Fuchs extensively annotated Rauwolf's three herbarium volumes — one of Fuchs's final scholarly interactions before his death in 1566.

FIRST PRINTED EDITION of Puff's distillation manual was produced in Augsburg — the same city where Rauwolf would serve as city physician a century later and where Widemann would sell books to Rudolf II.

Arnald of Villanova established the distillation tradition at Montpellier (c.1300). Rondelet inherited this institutional legacy and reportedly 'diffused the technique of distillation.' Not direct student-teacher but institutional continuity across 250 years at the same university.
Rauwolf sold his Levantine herbarium volumes directly to Rudolf II for 310 Reichstaler. These volumes were later looted by Swedish troops in the 1648 sack of Prague.

Brunschwig's Kleines Destillierbuch was published in Czech in 1559 in Olomouc (translated by Jan Jevicky Cerny, printed by Jan Gunther). Schaffner was born in Olomouc c.1564 — five years after this publication. Schaffner later trained Horcicky in distillation. No direct evidence Schaffner used this text, but the geographic and professional overlap is strong.

Brunschwig's Senf (mustard) entry (fol. 109v) describes distilling mustard seeds after vinegar maceration. Horcicky's commercial product was Aqua Sinapis (distilled mustard water). Puff's Büchlein has NO mustard chapter. The Brunschwig-Horcicky connection through mustard distillation is circumstantial but specific. No surviving Horcicky recipe for comparison.

Gmunden enrolled at Vienna in 1400; Galeazzo taught medicine at Vienna until 1405. They overlapped at the university for 5 years. Galeazzo performed the first Viennese anatomical dissection in 1404, during Gmunden's student years. As an Arts student, Gmunden would have been in the same institutional environment as the medical faculty's most prominent Italian professor.

Gmunden died in 1442, bequeathing his astronomical/mathematical manuscripts and instruments to the University of Vienna. Peuerbach enrolled in 1446. There were NO astronomy professors during Peuerbach's student years — Gmunden's bequeathed library and instruments sustained the tradition across the 4-year gap. Peuerbach built directly on Gmunden's foundation to create the 'First Viennese School of Mathematics' (named by Tannstetter, 1514).

Puff was born c.1400-1401 and first appears as Dean of the Medical Faculty in 1435, meaning he was at Vienna as a student and then faculty member from roughly the early 1420s. Gmunden was a senior Arts faculty master throughout this period (Dean 1423, Vice-chancellor after 1425). Puff would have studied natural philosophy (Physica, Meteorologica) under Arts faculty masters like Gmunden before entering the Medical faculty. The theoretical foundation for Puff's distillation work — elements, qualities, transformation — was taught in the Arts faculty that Gmunden dominated.
